name: MathlibAnnex.aeConstants_eq_of_open_overlap
title: Identifying constants on an open overlap

content.display_title: Identifying constants on an open overlap
content.one_sentence_role: Uses positive measure to find a point where both almost-everywhere equalities hold.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $X$ have a topology and a measurable structure, and let $\mu$ be a measure that assigns positive measure to every nonempty open set. Let $Y$ be any set, $u:X\to Y$, and $c,d\in Y$. Suppose $V,W\subseteq X$ are open, $V\cap W\ne\varnothing$, and
$$u=c\quad\mu|_V\text{-almost everywhere},\qquad
u=d\quad\mu|_W\text{-almost everywhere}.$$
Then $c=d$.
content.assumptions: No topology or measurable structure on $Y$ is required. There is no Haar, finite-measure, or Borel-compatibility assumption. Openness and nonempty overlap are used through positivity of that overlap, rather than through an assumed measurable-set identity.
content.conclusion: The two constants coincide as elements of $Y$. A selected point of $V\cap W$ need not satisfy either equality; positivity permits choosing a point outside both exceptional sets.
content.proof_summary: Restrict both equalities to the intersection, combine them there, and use positive measure to obtain a common good point.

proof_steps.text:
**Restrict the equalities.** Put $O=V\cap W$. Monotonicity of restriction transports the first almost-everywhere equality from $V$ to $O$, and the second from $W$ to $O$. Their conjunction holds almost everywhere for $\mu|_O$:
$$u(y)=c\ \text{and}\ u(y)=d\qquad\text{for }\mu|_O\text{-almost every }y.$$
Taking this finite conjunction is legitimate without any countable-cover assumption.

**Choose a good point.** The set $O$ is nonempty and open, so $0<\mu(O)$. The [positive-measure existence lemma](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Restrict.lean#L416-L419) applied to the preceding conjunction supplies a point $y\in O$ at which both equalities hold. Therefore
$$c=u(y)=d.$$
This is the step that would fail if the overlap merely contained a point but had measure zero.

content.lean_realization_notes: As throughout the gluing argument, $u=c$ almost everywhere on $V$ means almost everywhere for the restricted measure $\mu|_V$. The measure of the overlap may be infinite; only its being nonzero is needed.
